brief.head: Just do stuff
brief.text: Amit Varma learns by plung­ing in and work­ing out first prin­ci­ples later. His gyan, he said, comes from bum­bling through: “Just do stuff and you’ll learn from it.” {072-C14}

brief.head: Hearing a drought
brief.text: Bernie Krause recorded one Californian spot from 2004 to 2015. Eyes missed the species lost in a drought; “the sound­scape cap­tured ev­ery­thing”, Varma said. {072-S02}

brief.head: Thinking on paper
brief.text: Adam Smith could not have had his thoughts[[x6]] be­fore books, Varma ar­gued. Writing let him build lay­ers of thought upon ear­lier lay­ers, mak­ing him a bet­ter thinker. {072-C07}

brief.head: A voice in your head
brief.text: Radio must please five peo­ple[[x3]] in a car, Varma said, so it stays broad. A pod­cast is a voice in your head[[x4]], in­ti­mate enough to go deep. {072-C09}

brief.head: One format at a time
brief.text: Ajay Shah learnt to write pa­pers[[x5]], then op-eds, then blog posts, then books, spend­ing a cou­ple of years in­side each. Now all of them are “stored in my skull”. {072-S13}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the forms that shape art
lead.head: Thinking outside the vinyl

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 72

body: Why does a pop song last three min­utes, an album forty and a fea­ture film ninety? Not be­cause au­di­ences pre­ferred them, Amit Varma ar­gued in this week’s episode. Each form grew out of a con­straint, and most of those con­straints are gone.
Ajay Shah of­fered a line from Winston Churchill: “We make our build­ings and then our build­ings make us[[x1]].”
Varma has his own ver­sion. “I say form shapes con­tent, and con­tent shapes char­ac­ter,” he said. {072-C01}

He learnt it from his own pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*. A five-minute show can be shal­low; a ten-hour one de­mands that you read all the guest’s books and lis­ten with­out in­ter­rupt­ing, and that, he said, makes you a dif­fer­ent kind of per­son.
## Born of con­straint
The rule runs through na­ture. Rainforest birds re­peat calls in a nar­row band so that some­thing gets through; birds near the for­est floor call low.
Music, too, takes the shape of its room, Varma said, fol­low­ing David Byrne. Out in the open, rhythm car­ries, so out­door music is per­cus­sive.
In gothic cathe­drals, where a note hangs in the air for more than four sec­onds, music grew slow and har­mon­i­cally sim­ple. In crowded, clut­tered clubs it could be com­plex. Arenas favour metal.

Storage did the rest. The 78 RPM record held three min­utes, hence the three-minute pop song. Columbia’s LP, which Varma dated to 1948, held about twenty min­utes a side, hence the forty-minute album.
To those nos­tal­gic for the con­cept album, his reply: “Dude, the con­cept album came about be­cause there was a con­straint in the stor­age.” {072-C05}

The con­ven­tions out­lived the lim­its. Shah saw “pow­er­ful con­form­ist forces” at work; Varma, a se­lec­tion ef­fect, since an eight-minute song got no radio play un­less you were al­ready Pink Floyd.
## Pages and screens
Writing fol­lowed the same path. Books set­tled be­tween 100 and 300 pages, op-eds at 800 words. Blogging in the early 2000s freed Varma from both: he could write 80 words or 8,000.
On screen, a 90-minute fea­ture film is a short story, he ar­gued, and a stream­ing se­ries is a novel. {072-C08}
As for short at­ten­tion spans, he pointed out that peo­ple now binge eight hours of a se­ries at a stretch.
## A golden age

The final part of the episode turned to money. Creators now own the means of pro­duc­tion, Varma said, face no gate­keep­ers and no con­straint of form, and can reach and earn from their au­di­ences di­rectly. {072-C10}
That frees them from the old need to scale, when only the very top artists earned a liv­ing. A thou­sand true fans pay­ing $100 a year, in Kevin Kelly’s sum, is enough.
Shah asked whether this was sur­vivor bias. Varma said no: more than a lakh Indian cre­ators earn be­tween one and ten lakh ru­pees a month.
He went fur­ther. With more peo­ple alive, more leisure and cheap tools, he ar­gued, there should be more ac­tive cre­ators today than in all ear­lier his­tory com­bined.
Shah had a worry, half in jest: “Owing to the short­age of fol­low­ers, the pro­duc­tion of lead­ers has been dis­con­tin­ued.” {072-J11}

Varma ob­jected that not ev­ery­one is a cre­ator. Shah did the sums: about ten to the eighth po­ten­tial fol­low­ers and ten to the fifth cre­ators, “so there’s still like an av­er­age of thou­sand each”.

second.label: The limits of print
second.head: Too big to bind
second.deck: Robert Caro wrote a million words; the printers could bind only 800,000

pic.caption: Jane Jacobs at a West Village press conference in 1961

body: Amit Varma counts *The Power Broker*, Robert Caro’s bi­og­ra­phy of Robert Moses, among his favourite books. {072-R11} Caro de­liv­ered it to his pub­lisher, Robert Gottlieb, at one mil­lion words.[[x2]]

Gottlieb asked his print­ers what they could do. The most they could bind, they said, with­out the book fall­ing apart was 800,000 words. So a 200,000-word sec­tion on Jane Jacobs, “a hero to both you and me”, as Varma told Ajay Shah, was sim­ply cut. {072-S10}

Today, Varma said, such a sec­tion would be up­loaded or pub­lished as a book of its own. Then it was lost to his­tory. Every printed book, he added, has a floor and a ceil­ing: most run be­tween 100 and 300 pages.

quote.text: But at that time it’s just gone. It’s just lost to his­tory.

third.head: Solos born of majboori

pic.caption: Amit Varma on how jazz got its solos

body: Jazz sounds the way it does be­cause of where it began, Amit Varma said. Early jazz was played in venues with­out am­pli­fi­ca­tion, so the loud­est in­stru­ments won. {072-S06}
That is why the trum­pet be­came pop­u­lar, and why the banjo was pre­ferred to the acous­tic gui­tar. The gui­tar came back only when am­pli­fi­ca­tion ar­rived.

Improvisation had a prac­ti­cal start too. The early bands played for dancers, and when the writ­ten music ran out, the dancers still wanted to dance. {#dancers} “They’re pay­ing cus­tomers, you gotta do what you gotta do,” Varma said. So the band stretched out with solos.
“So it was al­most as com­ing out of ma­j­boori,” he said. “Today if they don’t im­pro­vise, we’ll de­mand our money back.”

p2.deck: Songs, books and films were shaped by constraints that no longer apply, Amit Varma argued, chapter by chapter

box.title: A book Varma gives away
box.text: Amit Varma calls David Byrne’s *How Music Works* a mas­ter­piece, and gives it to ev­ery­one he meets. The book shows how rooms and tech­nol­ogy, from gothic cathe­drals to CBGB’s, shaped the music made in them. {072-R04}

sections.label: Understand form
sections.head: Listen to understand
sections.caption: long conversations and listening
body: When Amit Varma started *The Seen and the Unseen*, he as­sumed that peo­ple have short at­ten­tion spans[[x10]], that you must hook them early, and that an episode can­not run past 10 or 15 min­utes. All of it, he said, was wrong[[x9]].

The show grew from sin­gle-subject episodes of 15 or 20 min­utes into three-hour deep dives, then into oral his­to­ries of eight hours and more. A re­cent one ran ten and a half hours. Ajay Shah said he was still wait­ing for his gold medal. Until the pod­cast ends, Varma replied, he is “the pro­vi­sional gold”. {072-J02}

In an essay, *A Meditation on Form*, he worked out that this was not the same thing made longer. {072-R02} A five-minute show can be shal­low. A seven- or eight-hour one de­mands all the guest’s books, knowl­edge of their field and a sense of their life. {072-S01}
## Listening with­out ego
It de­mands lis­ten­ing. “The key value that I learned from doing those long episodes is that you sim­ply never in­ter­rupt,” Varma said.
He in­voked Stephen Covey: we lis­ten to re­spond, we don’t lis­ten to un­der­stand. In a long con­ver­sa­tion, he said, you have to lis­ten to un­der­stand, with no room for ego. {072-J13}
That lis­ten­ing pro­duces deeper, more re­laxed con­tent, and that, he said, changes the per­son doing it. {072-C01}
~ It works the other way too. Some con­tent suits only one form: rapid-fire ques­tions need five min­utes, depth needs hours.

quote.text: The key to hav­ing a suc­cess­ful deep episode is that you allow the per­son to sink into their thoughts.

sections.label: The sound of rooms
sections.head: Rooms that wrote the music
sections.caption: how venues and storage shaped music
body: Amit Varma would pick one place and time to visit: CBGB’s in New York in 1975[[x11]], where American punk and al­ter­na­tive rock were born. The club was crowded, clut­tered and noisy. “And this was a fea­ture, not a bug,” he said, be­cause the mess ab­sorbed sound and killed re­ver­ber­a­tion[[x12]], mak­ing room for har­mon­i­cally com­plex music. {072-S03}

The same logic de­fends AC/DC’s Angus Young, mocked for one kind of sound and three or four chords. In vast are­nas you need a wall of sound, Varma re­called a gui­tarist telling Rick Beato, and for that Young’s style is per­fect. {072-S04}
There is no hi­er­ar­chy here, Varma said: Western clas­si­cal music is not more evolved than drum­ming. {072-C04}
The Beatles left the stage, Ajay Shah noted, partly be­cause the am­pli­fi­ca­tion of the day could not beat scream­ing fans, and they were head­ing to *A Day in the Life*.
## Thirty-second songs

New plat­forms bring new rules. Spotify pays once a track has played 30 sec­onds, so Vulfpeck re­leased *Sleepify*, an album of 30-second songs for fans to loop as they slept. {#sleepify} The band made a fair bit of money until Spotify caught on.

~ TikTok counts a liked video as liked audio, so mu­si­cians are now told to be as in­dul­gent as they like, as long as they de­liver: “Give me that fif­teen sec­ond hook I can put on TikTok.” {072-S09}

quote.text: There’s no hi­er­ar­chy, there’s no value judg­ment. Particular kinds of music sound the way they do be­cause of cir­cum­stances.

sections.label: The written word
sections.head: Eighty words or eight thousand
sections.caption: breaking free of the 800-word op-ed
body: Before the print­ing press, Amit Varma said, writ­ing was lim­ited by mem­ory and by cum­ber­some scrolls. He showed *Der Edelstein*, an early printed book by Ulrich Boner. {072-R10}
Print then fixed the forms. Books set­tled be­tween 100 and 300 pages; op-eds at 700 or 800 words, a thou­sand at most.
As a young would-be writer in the 1990s, Varma saw only two op­tions: 800-word op-eds for the *Times of India*[[x13]] or the *Indian Express*, or a book of around 200 pages.
## Blogging’s re­lease
Blogging in the early 2000s was a re­lease. “I was not bound by form. I could write some­thing in eighty words, I could write some­thing in eight thou­sand words,” he said. {072-S12}
Nor was he bound by the news cycle or a gate­keeper. He av­er­aged five posts a day for five years, about 8,000 posts, many just a line and a link. {#posts}
Social media later split blog­ging apart, he said: micro-blogging went to Twitter, per­sonal posts to Facebook and Instagram. Newsletters re­vived it, let­ting a writer keep read­ers for life.
~ Ajay Shah learnt pa­pers, op-eds, blogs and books one at a time, and now switches be­tween them at will. {072-S13} With great mod­esty, Varma said, he had left out his lat­est form: YouTube.

quote.text: The fact that he can have the thoughts he did is that by writ­ing, he is ac­tu­ally mak­ing him­self a bet­ter thinker.

sections.label: Screens and voices
sections.head: Films are short stories
sections.caption: the feature film as a short story
body: When Amit Varma wanted to be a film­maker, the forms on offer were the 90-minute Hollywood film, the three-hour Bollywood film and the half-hour TV show: 24 min­utes of con­tent and two three-minute ad breaks. {#doordarshan}
A 90-minute fea­ture, he ar­gued, is a short story, not a novel: one dom­i­nant nar­ra­tive arc, one ten­sion. {072-C08}

Streaming changed that. His favourite show, *The Wire*, made no at­tempt to hook the viewer, used no music be­yond what played in the scene, and let fif­teen or six­teen major char­ac­ters un­fold over sea­sons. {#wire}
What a 300-page book can do, he said, can now be done on screen.
## Closer and closer

Distance mat­ters too. In a cin­ema, the screen is far from the viewer and the cam­era roughly as far from the actor, which suits west­erns and car chases. {#cinema} Television sits a cou­ple of me­tres away, which suits *Friends* and *Seinfeld*. A YouTube video is in your hand, all close-ups.
A ten-hour con­ver­sa­tion, he added, is not ten one-hour ones: the rhythm is dif­fer­ent.
~ His al­most ten-hour episode with Rajeshwari Sengupta, *The Life and Times of the Indian Economy*, has passed 50,000 views on YouTube, though it is a thumb­nail and two peo­ple talk­ing. {072-S14}

quote.text: Actually a fea­ture film of ninety min­utes is equal to a short story. It’s not a novel.

sections.label: The golden age
sections.head: A thousand fans, no gatekeeper
sections.caption: the five changes for creators
body: Ajay Shah set up the ques­tion with a line from Stewart Brand: “We are as gods and we might as well learn to live like that.” Any teenager in her bed­room, he said, can now make a ten-hour video. How, he asked, does one find an au­di­ence?
Amit Varma listed five changes. Creators have the means of pro­duc­tion[[x14]], face no gate­keep­ers, are free of form, reach au­di­ences di­rectly and earn from them di­rectly. {072-C10}

The old model was clumsy. A news­pa­per gath­ered readers’ eye­balls, sold them to ad­ver­tis­ers and passed the writer a sliver, be­cause mi­cro­pay­ments had too much fric­tion. And your at­ten­tion is not free, Varma said: time is money.
## No need to scale

Once, only the very top artists earned any­thing; the medi­ocre artist starved in an attic. Kevin Kelly’s an­swer, in 2009[[x15]], was a thou­sand true fans pay­ing $100 a year. {072-R19} Li Jin’s was a hun­dred pay­ing $1,000.
Bari Weiss, “a fel­low win­ner of the Bastiat Prize”, started *The Free Press* on Substack; Varma had read that it is now val­ued at $100 mil­lion. {#weiss}
Is this sur­vivor bias? No, Varma told Shah: more than a lakh Indian cre­ators earn be­tween one and ten lakh ru­pees a month. {#lakh}
~ Miss Excel, who teaches Excel while danc­ing on Instagram, be­came a star. “Any gate­keeper would laugh her out of the room,” Varma said. {072-S15}

quote.text: Kelly’s point is you don’t need to scale any­more.
My sense is that we are liv­ing a golden age of all kinds of cre­ative arts. We should have Beethovens and Bachs and Kumar Gandharvas all around us. We should have a Shakespeare in every nukkad.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A poetry newsletter, a symphony on a disc, and a star at the airport

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on poetry, print and Delhi before 1857
stories.head: Verse that sold the newspapers
body: Between about 1801 and 1857, Delhi was a city in tran­si­tion. Amit Varma, draw­ing on Swapna Liddle’s *The Broken Script*, one of his favourite his­tory books, de­scribed what hap­pened when news­pa­pers and news­let­ters took off. {072-R14}

For some rea­son Varma could not ex­plain, po­etry was hugely pop­u­lar. “Newspapers would pub­lish sha­yari[[x16]] be­cause peo­ple would buy news­pa­pers to read them,” he said. The em­peror Zafar’s verses ap­peared[[x17]], but so did other poets’. {072-S11}
Ajay Shah was struck by some­thing else: “Unimaginable that an em­peror would com­pose po­etry.”

Then there were the mushairas, where poets gath­ered to re­cite to one an­other. One en­tre­pre­neur, much crit­i­cised in his time for his com­mer­cial in­stincts, de­cided that this had to be pre­served. He was en­joy­ing it so much, he rea­soned, that oth­ers would love it too.
So he began pub­lish­ing news­let­ters of all the poems re­cited at a mushaira, with an essay on mat­ters of form at the start.
Varma saw forms stacked on forms: a mushaira in a phys­i­cal space, a news­let­ter made pos­si­ble by the print­ing press, and out of the two, a new form of learn­ing.

Before that, Varma said, a stu­dent learnt po­etry piece­meal: one per­son re­cited a poem, then an­other. Now there were crit­i­cal es­says and col­lec­tions. Readers were ex­posed to “a large LLM, as it were”, and learnt much faster. {072-J08}
~ “It’s mirac­u­lous,” he said. It was al­most like what the in­ter­net did for his own gen­er­a­tion.
stories.why: A new medium laid over an old one can change how fast peo­ple learn. Varma set the mushaira news­let­ter be­side the in­ter­net: each turned a scat­tered, chance en­counter with an art into a fast, sys­tem­atic ed­u­ca­tion.
stories.postscript: Lest gos­sip seem mod­ern: Rahul Matthan told Varma, in an­other episode, that 19th-century English news­pa­pers were full of smut.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Delhi’s poetry newsletters

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the arbitrary origins of a standard
stories.head: The disc that Beethoven measured
body: When Philips and Sony came to­gether to in­vent the com­pact disc, Sony’s pres­i­dent was shown a disc by Philips that held sixty min­utes and could go higher. He asked for sev­enty-four. {#cdsixty}
Why sev­enty-four? Amit Varma put the ques­tion to Ajay Shah, who got it at once: “The ninth of Beethoven?”
“Yeah, he was a big fan of Ludwig van Beethoven and Beethoven’s ninth sym­phony is sev­enty four min­utes,” Varma said. {072-S07}

~ So for that ar­bi­trary rea­son, a CD held 74 min­utes of music; later CDs could hold more. The point, for Varma, was how such lim­its be­come con­ven­tions[[x18]]. There is no log­i­cal rea­son left to think in forty-minute al­bums, he said, but bands still do.
stories.why: Standards that feel nat­u­ral often have ar­bi­trary ori­gins: the ca­pac­ity of a whole medium was set by one executive’s favourite sym­phony. Listeners who mourn the con­cept album, Varma ar­gued, are mourn­ing a stor­age con­straint. {072-C05}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the length of a CD

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Pink Floyd and the one-hour block
stories.head: One album, one hour of FM
body: Looking back at the shifts from the 78 RPM record to the 33 RPM to the CD, Ajay Shah was struck by how few mu­si­cians ever broke with con­ven­tion. {072-C06}

There were ex­cep­tions. Pink Floyd’s *Echoes*, he thought, takes up the whole of side two of *Meddle*. But mostly, he guessed, “there are pow­er­ful con­form­ist forces that want you to fit into a main­stream world.”

Then there was *Dark Side of the Moon*[[x19]]. He had read that in the early years of FM radio, the album was a per­fect match for the medium. Stations could play some ads, play the en­tire album, play some more ads, and that made a one-hour block. {072-S08}
~ Amit Varma added a se­lec­tion ef­fect. Unless you were al­ready a su­per­star like Pink Floyd, an eight-minute song sim­ply did not get played on radio.

quote.text: Play the en­tire Dark Side of the Moon, and then you play some ads, and that’s a one hour block.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Dark Side of the Moon on FM radio

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on fame in the age of the niche
stories.head: Famous in a crowd of one
body: It hap­pens often, Amit Varma said. He is at an air­port, and some­one stops him to thank him for his work. {072-S16}
“Nobody around has a faintest clue who I am,” he said. “They’re all look­ing and going, who’s this guy? But for this per­son, I’m Shah Rukh Khan.”

Fame, in his telling, now lives in small cir­cles of de­vo­tion. He named the Peter Cat Recording Company, loved by him and his crew Nomsita and Vaishnav: “never gonna be the Beatles in terms of scale”, but the Beatles to their fans. {072-J21}
~ Mainstream adu­la­tion, the kind in which peo­ple build tem­ples to Amitabh Bachchan, may have had its day, he said. {#temples} The in­ti­mate kind, he ex­pects, will be­come more and more com­mon.
stories.why: Fame has not van­ished; it has moved into niches. A cre­ator un­known to the crowd can be a star to the one per­son who stops him, and that de­vo­tion, Varma ar­gues, is what pays. {072-C12}
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah had his own mo­ment: a CRPF man at air­port se­cu­rity, faced with a back­pack hold­ing a tri­pod, asked, “YouTube karte ho?” {072-S17}

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 72. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Ludwig van Beethoven (Joseph Karl Stieler, public domain); David Byrne (Raph_PH, CC BY 2.0); Jane Jacobs (Phil Stanziola, public domain); Stephen Covey (Sterling.morris (talk), public domain); Angus Young (MATT BECKER, CC BY-SA 3.0); Robert Caro (Larry D. Moore, CC BY 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple, Open Library and Spotify.

shelf.why: Amit’s essay on how form dic­tates con­tent: long-form pod­cast­ing is a dif­fer­ent ac­tiv­ity from short-form, not a longer ver­sion of it, and its pa­tience, lis­ten­ing and cu­rios­ity changed him as a host and per­haps as a per­son.

shelf.title: Earwitness to Place
shelf.creator: Bernie Krause (interviewed by Erin Robinsong)
shelf.why: The source for how habi­tat shapes bird­song and how a sound­scape re­vealed species loss dur­ing a drought.

shelf.title: How Music Works
shelf.creator: David Byrne
shelf.why: The best book Amit has read about music, which he gives to ev­ery­one: it shows how venues and tech­nol­ogy, from cathe­drals to CBGB’s, shaped the music played in them, feed­ing his ob­ses­sion with how form shapes the world.

shelf.title: Nuno Bettencourt interviewed by Rick Beato
shelf.creator: Rick Beato
shelf.why: Makes the case that AC/DC’s sim­ple wall of sound is ideal for are­nas, a re­minder to judge music against its cir­cum­stances.

shelf.title: How Bing Crosby Made Silicon Valley Possible
shelf.creator: Ted Gioia
shelf.why: Shows how a new tech­nol­ogy pro­duced a new style of singing: soft, close-up and in­ti­mate, as with Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra.

shelf.title: Sleepify
shelf.creator: Vulfpeck
shelf.why: An album of 30-second tracks meant to loop all night while fans slept, and it made the band money until Spotify caught on.

shelf.title: 100BeatlesX30
shelf.creator: The Pocket Gods
shelf.why: A large batch of 30-second Beatles cov­ers, an­other re­sponse to the same stream­ing rule.

shelf.title: The Seven Basic Plots (Episode 69)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Makes the point that a con­straint doesn’t stop great work.

shelf.title: Der Edelstein
shelf.creator: Ulrich Boner
shelf.why: A vis­ual start­ing point for the story of how print­ing and dis­tri­bu­tion shaped writ­ing.

shelf.title: The Power Broker
shelf.creator: Robert Caro
shelf.why: Caro’s mas­ter­piece works on three lev­els: a bi­og­ra­phy of Robert Moses, a bi­og­ra­phy of New York re­shaped by top-down plan­ning, and a study of how power cor­rupts an ide­al­is­tic man.

shelf.title: Rahul Matthan Seeks the Protocol (Episode 360 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Rahul Matthan makes the strong­est case that Aadhaar has pri­vacy built into its de­sign, the view Ajay chal­lenges.

shelf.title: Swapna Liddle and the Many Shades of Delhi (Episode 367 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Historian Swapna Liddle on Delhi: Delhi College, po­etry in the city’s news­pa­pers and mushaira news­let­ters, and how the British used ed­u­ca­tion to push their nar­ra­tives about Indian his­tory.

shelf.title: The Broken Script
shelf.creator: Swapna Liddle
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite his­tory books: Delhi from 1803 to 1857, when Persian col­lapsed, print and news­pa­pers boomed and po­etry was pop­u­lar cul­ture, until it all ended in 1857.

shelf.title: The Wire
shelf.why: A show that ig­nores the habits of tra­di­tional cin­ema (no hook, no back­ground score, fif­teen or six­teen major char­ac­ters, a story un­fold­ing slowly over sea­sons) and proved that TV can do what a novel does.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A nearly ten-hour tour with Rajeswari Sengupta of India’s growth episodes and fail­ures and the costs of its post-independence eco­nomic choices.

shelf.title: If You Are a Creator, This Is Your Time
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s five rea­sons this is a good time for cre­ators: they own the means of pro­duc­tion, need no gate­keep­ers, face no con­straint of form, reach au­di­ences di­rectly and can mon­e­tise di­rectly.

shelf.title: 1000 True Fans
shelf.creator: Kevin Kelly
shelf.why: Kevin Kelly’s ar­gu­ment that cre­ators don’t need scale: a thou­sand true fans pay­ing $100 a year is a liv­ing, wher­ever in the world they are.

shelf.title: 100 True Fans
shelf.creator: Li Jin
shelf.why: Li Jin’s more con­cen­trated ver­sion of Kevin Kelly’s idea: a hun­dred fans pay­ing $1,000 a year give a cre­ator the same in­come from a smaller, more com­mit­ted au­di­ence.

shelf.title: The Free Press
shelf.creator: Bari Weiss
shelf.why: Bari Weiss’s pub­li­ca­tion, ev­i­dence that one per­son start­ing a news­let­ter can build a very large busi­ness on plat­forms where cre­ators own their au­di­ence, with­out a mass-media gate­keeper.

shelf.title: Shephali Bhatt Is Searching for the Incredible (Episode 391 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Journalist Shephali Bhatt on find­ing her sense of pur­pose through in­di­vid­u­als in news­rooms that treated jour­nal­ists as a cost cen­tre, which Amit finds very mov­ing.

shelf.title: The Honest Broker
shelf.creator: Ted Gioia
shelf.why: Amit calls Gioia a deep meta-thinker about music and the music busi­ness.

shelf.title: Rick Beato’s YouTube channel
shelf.creator: Rick Beato
shelf.why: A great music chan­nel that Amit en­joys a lot and loves, though he says it isn’t much about think­ing on form.

shelf.title: The Design of Everyday Things
shelf.creator: Don Norman
shelf.why: Norman shows that ev­ery­thing around us looks and works the way it does for rea­sons we have stopped notic­ing, and that noth­ing is beau­ti­ful un­less it is also beau­ti­fully func­tional, a les­son for en­gi­neer­ing too.

shelf.title: Ten Years Gone
shelf.creator: Led Zeppelin
shelf.why: Ajay’s pick for the great­est Led Zeppelin song that is not widely known.

laughs.text: Ajay opens by call­ing Amit ‘more than just an atom in a ki­netic the­ory of gases’ since he also con­tem­plates the the­ory. Amit: ‘If I was sexy, I would be an atom bomb.’ When Ajay pushes the metaphor, Amit says the an­swer to why atoms bounce around is ‘we have no idea. Life is prob­a­bly mean­ing­less, we’re all gonna die.’

On the ten-and-a-half-hour episode. Ajay: ‘I’m still wait­ing for my gold medal.’ Amit: ‘until the pod­cast comes to an end, you can’t get the gold medal. You are the pro­vi­sional gold at the mo­ment.’
Pointing out the bird­song in the back­ground: ‘The twit­ter­ing of birds, not twit­ter... or per­haps we should call the Xing of birds.’
On rain­for­est birds that re­peat the same nar­row-frequency call so some­thing gets through: ‘Like so many colum­nists, in fact.’
On why open-air pro­ces­sions are per­cus­sive: ‘You will not hear khay­als and thum­ris while peo­ple are march­ing to the beach.’
Amit’s off-colour aside about the au­thor of Der Edelstein: ‘Apparently his wife used to say that every morn­ing I wake up and I find that Boner has a boner. But leav­ing that aside...’
On early croon­ers singing softly into the mic: ‘much as some pod­cast­ers can do with their dy­namic mi­cro­phones.’
Amit calls the mushaira news­let­ters ex­po­sure to ‘a large LLM, as it were’, using AI vo­cab­u­lary for a 19th-century reader’s sam­ple size.
On binge-watching: ‘For those of us who have of­fice, we miss of­fice the next day. I don’t have to.’

Ajay: ‘owing to the short­age of fol­low­ers, the pro­duc­tion of lead­ers has been dis­con­tin­ued.’ Amit ob­jects that not ev­ery­one is a cre­ator, and Ajay does the maths: about 10^8 po­ten­tial fol­low­ers and 10^5 cre­ators, ‘so there’s still like an av­er­age of thou­sand each.’
Winston Churchill, quoted by Ajay: ‘we make our build­ings and then our build­ings make us.’
Stephen Covey: ‘we lis­ten to re­spond, we don’t lis­ten to un­der­stand.’ Amit uses it to de­scribe the lis­ten­ing long con­ver­sa­tions re­quire.
Stewart Brand, quoted by Ajay: ‘We are as gods and we might as well learn to live like that.’
Sturgeon’s Law, ‘ninety five per­cent of ev­ery­thing is crap’, which Amit cites while ar­gu­ing that great art is still being made in Instagram reels and TikTok.
Amit calls Bari Weiss ‘a fel­low win­ner of the Bastiat Prize.’
The Peter Cat Recording Company, loved by Amit and crew Nomsita and Vaishnav: ‘never gonna be the Beatles in terms of scale’, but the Beatles to their de­voted fans.
